pitch.kurz: A 22-person agency weighs AI agents against rehiring its ops coordinator.
pitch.text: I run Northfield Creative, a 22-person marketing agency in Denver. Our ops coordinator left on September 30. Most of her month went into client reports for 31 retainer clients, onboarding, invoice reminders and keeping Asana tidy. Rehiring costs about $73,700 a year fully loaded and took 9 weeks last time. A consultant quoted $12,500 to set up Claude agents that draft the reports, run onboarding and chase invoices, with an account manager approving everything, plus $1,430 a month to run it. I lean towards the agents and skipping the hire. What I'm not sure about: a third of her hours were people and office work no agent will do, and two reports already went out late this month. Do we replace the role with agents, rehire, or test first?
annahmen: Fictional example: the agency, the people and all numbers are made up for a demo.
The moderator answered the cross-examination for Dana in auto mode, from the documents.

optionen.text: Replace the role with the AI agent setup
Six-week pilot on the monthly reports, then decide on the hire

panel.warum: Does $29,660 in year one beat a $73,700 hire once the hidden hours are counted?

Client contracts, client data, and what happens when a report is wrong.
Does this change how the agency keeps and wins clients?

beitraege.text: The payback hangs on 101 hours a month that nobody has measured as saved. If they are real, the net is about $2,320 a month after $1,760 to run it, Priya's time included, and the $12,500 setup is back in roughly five and a half months. At half the hours it is $280 a month, about 45 months. Year one costs $33,620 against $73,700 for the hire, but the 51 hours of office and people work no agent covers are worth about $2,060 a month at her loaded rate, and nobody owns them. There is no stop date and no spending cap, and the care plan locks in $7,800 for 12 months, so I would test the reports first.

I wouldn't skip the hire on a quote alone: test the reports and open the recruiting in parallel, because six weeks of testing plus nine weeks of hiring leaves the seat empty for fifteen weeks. Even with the agents, year one costs $33,620 once you count Priya's time, and the 51 hours are still uncovered.

beitraege.text: What do the nine subcontractor clauses actually say, and will those clients approve Claude in writing before any of their data goes in? Is there a signed data processing agreement for your Claude account?

We know the clause from the MSAs: client data may only be processed by approved subcontractors. Whether an AI vendor counts, we don't know yet, and nobody has asked the nine. There is no Claude Team account and no data agreement yet, so none of their data is in there today. What the six people put into their personal AI accounts, we don't know.
Who takes the 51 hours a month of vendor, office and people work starting now, by name, and what do they drop to make room?
Nobody, honestly. Since September 30 the account managers cover reports and onboarding and I do the invoicing. Vendors, office and people work just slip. I don't have a name for it yet.
What is your hard spending cap and stop date, and which measured number, hours per report against today's 52, decides go or stop?

We haven't set a cap or a stop date. The 52 hours a month for reports are measured in her time tracker, so that is the number we could test against. What the agents would bring it down to, we don't know yet.
Will the consultant run a reports-only pilot at a fixed price, with seats and care plan cancelable after six weeks if it fails?
The quote only covers the full setup at $12,500 and a care plan with a 12-month minimum. I haven't asked for a reports-only pilot, so I don't know the price or whether they would do it.

A full-time search opened now commits $73,700 a year, plus $11,600 if you use a recruiter, before anyone knows whether 101 hours go away. If they do, what is left is a 51-hour job worth about $2,060 a month, not a $6,140 seat. The empty seat is also not a cash drain: it saves about $1,420 a week in loaded payroll, roughly $21,000 over fifteen weeks, so the real price of waiting is the late reports and the 51 orphaned hours. Bridge those with named cover capped at $2,060 a month and open the search at the pilot readout.

urteil.begruendung: No-Go for replacing the role with agents as pitched: all five vote no. Not because agents can't do the work. The 52 hours of monthly reports are measured and repeatable, and every member puts the reports pilot (option C) first. The plan fails on what surrounds the agents. Nine client contracts restrict who may process client data and nobody has asked those clients, there is no Claude account or data agreement yet, 51 hours a month of people, vendor and office work have no owner while reports are already late, and the quote locks in $12,500 plus a 12-month care plan before one real report has been drafted. Rehiring right away is not the answer either: it commits $73,700 a year before anyone knows whether 101 hours go away. The council's path is a priced, cancelable reports pilot with the legal and staffing gates cleared first.
